stem: Convertibility of rupee implies :

options.label: a
options.text: being able to convert rupee notes into gold

options.label: b
options.text: allowing the value of rupee to be fixed by market forces

options.label: c
options.text: freely permitting the conversion of rupee to other currencies and vice-versa

options.label: d
options.text: developing an international market for currencies in India

expl: Rupee convertibility means the free conversion of the rupee into foreign currencies and foreign currencies into rupees, without restrictions. Full convertibility of the rupee (on both the current account and the capital account) would mean no restriction on foreign capital entering or leaving India. As a result, adopting full convertibility would increase foreign investors’ confidence in the Indian economy and thereby raise inflows of foreign capital. Hence, achieving full convertibility of the Indian rupee is an important objective of India’s economic policy. It may be noted that since August 1994, the rupee has been fully convertible on the current account (on the trade account, it became partially convertible as early as March 1992). Regarding capital account convertibility, a committee was constituted in June 1997 under the chairmanship of S. S. Tarapore, which recommended a phased move towards capital account convertibility subject to certain conditions. Again, in March 2006, another committee (II) under S. S. Tarapore was formed to prepare a roadmap for capital account convertibility; after reviewing existing capital controls, it prepared a comprehensive, time-bound five-year plan in three phases for capital convertibility. Although capital account convertibility does not exist at present, the Reserve Bank follows a highly liberal policy with respect to various capital transactions.

expl: From 1975 to 1992, the exchange rate of the Indian rupee used to be determined on the basis of a basket of currencies of developed countries. This foreign-currency basket included the currencies of five countries/groups—United States dollar, Japan’s yen, the United Kingdom’s pound sterling, China’s Renminbi (Yuan), and the euro. From March 1992 to March 1993, a dual system of a market rate and an administered (official) rate was adopted, and from March 1993 onward, the exchange rate of the rupee has been determined on the basis of demand and supply in the market.

stem: at present the country has adopted-
expl: The then Finance Minister Manmohan Singh implemented the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) from 1992–93 on the current account. Under LERMS, 40% of foreign exchange earnings were converted at the exchange rate fixed by the Reserve Bank of India, and the remaining 60% at the market-determined rate. In 1993–94, the then Finance Minister Manmohan Singh declared the rupee fully convertible on the trade account (exports + imports). Moving further in this direction, in 1994–95 the rupee was made fully convertible on the current account of the balance of payments. At present, the rupee is fully convertible on the current account and partially convertible on the capital account.

stem: Who was awarded the nobel Prize in Economics in 1998?
expl: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded Amartya Sen the Nobel Prize in Economics for the year 1998 for his significant contribution to welfare economics. According to the Academy’s citation, his contributions to welfare economics helped in understanding the economic mechanisms related to famine and poverty. Among the books written by Amartya Sen, “Collective Choice and Social Welfare”, “The Idea of Justice”, and “On Ethics and Economics” are the most discussed. The Nobel Prize in Economics for 2019 was given to Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, and Michael Kremer for their “experimental approach to alleviating global poverty”, whereas the Nobel Prize in Economics for 2022 was given to Ben S. Bernanke, Douglas W. Diamond, and Philip H. Dybvig. The Nobel Prize in Economics for 2023 was awarded to Claudia Goldin. The Nobel Prize in Economics for 2024 was awarded to three American economists—Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, and James A. Robinson—for “studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity”. The Nobel Prize in Economics for 2025 has been jointly awarded to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion, and Peter Howitt.
